pass_a_gloss: Paul says somewhere to those who endured in the beginning, calling on them in agreement with the earlier endurance to carry second dangers, those because of the word: and call back to mind the earlier days, in which, having been illumined, you endured much athletic struggle of sufferings, on this side by reproaches and tribulations being made a theatre-show, on that side having become partners of those conducting themselves so. For you also co-suffered with my bonds, and the seizure of your belongings with joy you received, knowing that you have a stronger belonging and one remaining. Do not then cast off your freedom of speech, which has great wage-repayment. For of endurance you have need. Much, accordingly, we too now let us endure, struggle of sufferings, by reproaches and tribulations also being made a theatre-show, and with joy receiving the seizure of the belongings of ours; for we are convinced to have a stronger belonging, not of the earth, but not even of the body, but some unseen and bodiless one. For we look out not at the things being seen, beholding these as for a season, but those as age-long.
pass_b_english: Paul says somewhere to those who had endured at the beginning, urging them to bear the second dangers, the ones that come for the word's sake, in keeping with the endurance they had shown before: “But remember the earlier days, when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings: at times you were made a public spectacle by reproaches and afflictions, and at times you became partners of those who lived in that state. For you also suffered with me in my bonds, and you accepted the plundering of your property with joy, knowing that you have a better possession, and a lasting one. So do not throw away your boldness, which has a great reward. For you need endurance” (Hebrews 10:32-36).

Let us too, then, now endure “a great contest” “of sufferings”, being made a spectacle “by reproaches and afflictions”, and accepting “with joy” “the plundering of” our “property”. For we are persuaded that we have a “better” “possession”: not earthly, nor even bodily, but one that is invisible and incorporeal. For we look not at “the things that are seen” (2 Corinthians 4:18), since we see that these are “temporary” and those “eternal”.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 44); the old English was a digest: it rewrote the end of the Hebrews quotation ('that, doing God's will, you may receive the promise'), which Origen does not quote, and dropped his own application (a better possession that is invisible and incorporeal, and 2 Corinthians 4:18).
Origen re-uses Hebrews in short pieces; each piece is set in its own quotation marks as he quotes it, without repeating the citation.
